::: {callout-important}
## Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

**Methodology:** Since the Census (ACS) does not provide information about the immigration status of survey respondents, we trained a machine learning model on a smaller survey (SIPP) to impute undocumented status onto 2009-2019 ACS data.

**Finding:** Benchmarking our estimates of the undocumented population in the U.S. against the official DHS estimates highlights the limitations of machine learning imputation methods, particularly when there is distribution drift in the underlying population characteristics over time. This method overestimates the number of younger undocumented immigrants (ages 18-34) and underestimates the number of older undocumented immigrants (ages 35-54), with the gap between our estimates and DHS estimates widening over time.

:::

## Motivating Challenge

Methodology for estimating hidden populations (e.g. undocumented immigrants or students) has been a topic of debate as improvements are made throughout the last few decades.

Before deploying any advanced modeling, it is critical to understand the shape, missingness, and distributions of the raw Department of Homeland Security data. The primary objective for this post is to examine the demographic distribution of the DHS estimates from 2009-2019, specifically focusing on the age and gender composition of the undocumented population over time. 

Our goal is not to get as close to the official DHS estimates (there are simpler methods that result in more accurate aggregated estimates), but rather to assess the robustness of our machine learning method - being able to create estimates of the undocumented population is an interesting application of our research.

## Methodology & Data Pipelines

<div>

![Research Methodology diagram: Overview of sources, machine learning imputation method, data pipeline, and DHS comparisons workflow.](/media/methodology_blog.png){group="my-gallery" fig-align="center" width="95%"}

</div>

### Loading the Data

We'll start by pulling in the summary statistics and estimates from our database and our extracted DHS tables. Data preparation can be described in two steps:

1.  Training machine learning models on cleaned SIPP data to impute undocumented status in the ACS using gradient-boosted trees. This process is identical to what can be found [here](https://marioarceacosta.github.io/leading_xgboost_model.html) (and the current repository machine learning code can be found [here](https://github.com/MarioArceAcosta/ML-Causal-Undocu-Research/tree/main/(Step%203)%20Machine%20Learning%20Estimations)).
2.  Creating a high-level snapshot of this data to be uploaded via SQL to Supabase for future use, alongside our extracted official DHS demographic tables.

### Imputed Distribution
Since the American Community Survey (ACS) does not directly ask about immigration status, we trained a machine learning algorithm on the demographic patterns in the 2008 Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) Wave 2 which did ask about immigration status, and then we applied the trained machine learning models to impute undocumented status within the ACS data for a later analysis (often referred to as a *downstream analysis).*

Because the demographic patterns of undocumented immigrants from 2008 differ from the demographic patterns of undocumented immigrants from the years 2009-2019, we need to assess how robust our machine learning models are to this change (referred to as *covariate* or *distribution drift*). To evaluate distribution drift, we need to compare a ground truth distribution with our estimated distribution.

:::{.callout-note}
**Note:** We later exclude the *55+* age bracket later in our analysis for visual purposes.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: etl-prep
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
library(DBI)
library(RPostgres)

# 1. Feature engineering and aggregation

ACS_foreign_gbm <- read.csv("G:/Shared drives/Undocu Research/Data/ACS_foreign_gbm.csv")

acs_summary <- ACS_foreign_gbm %>%
  filter(bpl_foreign == 1) %>% 
  
  mutate(
    age_bracket = case_when(
      age < 18 ~ "Under 18",
      age >= 18 & age < 25 ~ "18-24",
      age >= 25 & age < 35 ~ "25-34",
      age >= 35 & age < 45 ~ "35-44",
      age >= 45 & age < 55 ~ "45-54",
      age >= 55 ~ "55+",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(age_bracket != "Under 18") %>%
  group_by(
    year, 
    statefip, 
    bpld, 
    age_bracket, 
    fem
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    # summing 'perwt' now gives us the Total Foreign-Born Population.
    total_foreign_born_pop = sum(perwt, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # 1. High Recall Estimates
    high_recall_count = sum(perwt[gbm_high_recall == TRUE], na.rm = TRUE),
    high_recall_rate = high_recall_count / total_foreign_born_pop,
    
    # 2. High Probability Estimates
    high_prob_count = sum(perwt[gbm_high_prob == TRUE], na.rm = TRUE),
    high_prob_rate = high_prob_count / total_foreign_born_pop,
    
    # 3. Low Probability Estimates
    low_prob_count = sum(perwt[gbm_low_prob == TRUE], na.rm = TRUE),
    low_prob_rate = low_prob_count / total_foreign_born_pop,
    
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# 2. Push to supabase
con <- dbConnect(
  RPostgres::Postgres(),
  dbname = "postgres",
  host = "aws-1-us-east-2.pooler.supabase.com", 
  port = 6543,
  user = "postgres.dpuhypyqwupzesfkiplu",
  password = Sys.getenv("SUPABASE_PWD")
)

# Write the summary table to database
dbWriteTable(con, "acs_foreign_summary", acs_summary, overwrite = TRUE)

dbDisconnect(con)
```

### DHS Distribution (Baseline)

The DHS estimates of undocumented immigrants in the United States are often taken to be some of the most credible and officially recognized estimates. For this reason, we manually translate the estimates found in DHS report series - *Estimates of the Illegal Alien Population Residing in the United States -* into CSV files (public [DHS database](https://ohss.dhs.gov/topics/immigration/illegal/population-estimates)). Due to limited data consistency and granularity across the SIPP and ACS, we only extract and load the DHS total estimates and breakdowns by age and gender. For this same reason, as well as because of our sample characteristics, we exclude the *Under 18* age bracket in the DHS datasets.

:::{.callout-note}
**Data Gap Note:** DHS did not produce estimates for the year of **2013** due to a lack of data.
:::

```{r}
#| label: data-prep
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(DBI)
library(RPostgres)

# 1. Fetch ACS data from Supabase database
con <- dbConnect(
  RPostgres::Postgres(),
  dbname = "postgres",
  host = "aws-1-us-east-2.pooler.supabase.com", 
  port = 6543,
  user = "postgres.dpuhypyqwupzesfkiplu",
  password = Sys.getenv("SUPABASE_PWD"),
  connect_timeout = 10
)
acs_foreign_summary <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM acs_foreign_summary")
dbDisconnect(con)

# 2. Load DHS CSV data
dhs_male <- read_csv("Unauthorized Immigrant Population Estimates (Male) 2009-2022 - Unauthorized Immigrant Population Estimates (Male) 2009-2022.csv") %>%
  filter(Year >= 2009 & Year <= 2019) %>%
  rename(year = Year, age_bracket = Age, population_count = Count) %>%
  mutate(gender = "Male")

dhs_female <- read_csv("Unauthorized Immigrant Population Estimates (Female) 2009-2022 - Unauthorized Immigrant Population Estimates (Female) 2009-2022.csv") %>%
  filter(Year >= 2009 & Year <= 2019) %>%
  rename(year = Year, age_bracket = Age, population_count = Count) %>%
  mutate(gender = "Female")

dhs_combined <- bind_rows(dhs_male, dhs_female) %>%
  mutate(
    age_bracket = str_trim(str_replace_all(age_bracket, '=|"', '')),
    dataset = "DHS Official"
  ) %>%
  filter(age_bracket != "Under 18", age_bracket != "Total", !is.na(year))

# 3. Prep ACS gender data
acs_combined <- acs_foreign_summary %>%
  # Change ACS sex codes to match DHS
  mutate(
    age_bracket = ifelse(age_bracket == "55+", "55 And Over", age_bracket),
    gender = case_when(
      fem == 1 ~ "Female",
      fem == 0 ~ "Male",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(age_bracket != "Under 18", gender != "Unknown", !is.na(year)) %>%
  group_by(year, age_bracket, gender) %>%
  summarise(population_count = sum(high_recall_count, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(dataset = "Imputed ACS")



# 4. Merge and offset
plot_data <- bind_rows(dhs_combined, acs_combined) %>%
  mutate(
    age_bracket = factor(age_bracket, levels = c("18-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-54", "55 And Over")),
    gender = factor(gender, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    
    
    fill_group = paste(gender, dataset, sep = " - "),
  
    age_numeric = as.numeric(age_bracket),
    plot_x = ifelse(dataset == "Imputed ACS", age_numeric - 0.2, age_numeric + 0.2)
  )
```

## Visualizing Demographic Trends

To establish a demographic baseline, we examine the age and gender composition of the undocumented population reported by DHS over the years 2009-2019. By stacking the male and female estimates, we can observe the total size of each age bracket alongside its gender distribution.

### Faceted/Overview Plots of DHS Demographics (Age & Gender)

```{r}
#| label: age-gender-faceted
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(ggplot2)
library(scales) 
library(plotly)

p_comparison_faceted <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = plot_x, y = population_count, fill = fill_group)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "black", alpha = 0.9, width = 0.35) +
  
  # Assign distinct colors to distinguish ACS from DHS visually
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Male - DHS Official"   = "#2471A3",
    "Female - DHS Official" = "#7FB3D5",
    "Male - Imputed ACS"   = "#BA4A00", 
    "Female - Imputed ACS" = "#F5B041"
  )) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 1:5,
    labels = levels(plot_data$age_bracket)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Population Estimates by Age and Gender: Imputed ACS vs DHS Official",
    x = "Age Bracket",
    y = "Total Population Estimate",
    fill = "Dataset & Gender"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, color = "black"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    
    panel.spacing = unit(2, "lines"), 
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", margin = margin(b = 10, t = 10)) 
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 3)

ggplotly(p_comparison_faceted, tooltip = c("fill", "y")) %>%
  layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.5, xanchor = "center", y = -0.1), margin = list(b = 60))
```

### Year-by-Year Interactive Composition

You can use the interactive chart below with the slider to track demographic shifts from 2009 to 2019. By pressing play, you can observe how the ACS estimates compare against the DHS estimates.

```{r}
#| label: age-gender-interactive
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(plotly)

p_interactive_comparison <- plot_ly(
  data = plot_data,
  x = ~plot_x,
  y = ~population_count,
  color = ~fill_group,
  colors = c(
    "Male - DHS Official"   = "#2471A3", 
    "Female - DHS Official" = "#7FB3D5", 
    "Male - Imputed ACS"   = "#BA4A00", 
    "Female - Imputed ACS" = "#F5B041"
  ),
  frame = ~year,          
  type = 'bar', 
  text = ~dataset,
  hovertemplate = '<b>%{text}</b><br>%{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>' 
) %>%
  layout(
    barmode = 'stack',    
    
    title = list(
      text = "<b>Interactive Comparison: Imputed ACS vs DHS Official</b>",
      font = list(family = "Arial", size = 16),
      x = 0.5 
    ),
    
    xaxis = list(
      title = "<b>Age Bracket</b>",
      tickvals = 1:5,
      ticktext = levels(plot_data$age_bracket),
      tickfont = list(size = 12)
    ),
    
    yaxis = list(
      title = "<b>Total Population Estimate</b>",
      tickformat = ",d", 
      range = c(0, max(
        plot_data %>% 
          group_by(year, plot_x) %>% 
          summarise(total = sum(population_count, na.rm=TRUE), .groups="drop") %>% 
          pull(total)
      ) * 1.1)
    ),
    
    
    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",  
      x = 0.5,            
      xanchor = "center",
      y = -0.5            
    ),
    
    margin = list(b = 160) 
  ) %>%
  animation_opts(
    frame = 1200,         
    transition = 500,     
    redraw = FALSE        
  ) %>%
  animation_slider(
    currentvalue = list(prefix = "<b>Year:</b> ", font = list(color = "black")),
    pad = list(t = 40)
  )

p_interactive_comparison
```

## Data Limitations

Comparing our ACS imputed estimates with the DHS estimates for the years 2009-2019 and across demographic categories revealed a known and important issue: distribution drift. [This report by the Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/race-and-ethnicity/2025/08/21/u-s-unauthorized-immigrant-population-reached-a-record-14-million-in-2023/) neatly explains how the demographic characteristics of undocumented immigrants in the United States have changed over the years. An example is the fact that the proportion of undocumented immigrants whose origin is Mexico has gone down over the years.

Since the machine learning imputation method learns the demographic patterns from a survey in 2008, and since the demographic characteristics have changed from 2009 to 2019, this method will incorrectly assign probabilities of undocumented status and imputations. This phenomenon is a common obstacle in machine learning for obtaining accurate classifications, and it is an obstacle that is difficult to resolve given the lack of publicly available data where vulnerable populations (i.e. undocumented immigrants) have self-reported information that could be used in social science.

### Key Findings

So, the result of this distribution drift is that we have:

1.  Overestimated the number of younger undocumented immigrants (age brackets 18-24 and 25-34).

2.  Underestimated the number of older undocumented immigrants (age brackets 35-44 and 45-54).

It is important to also note that this gap between our estimates and the DHS estimates gets larger throughout the years. This may reflect how the demographic distribution of undocumented immigrants in the United States has changed since 2008, which would explain the deteriorating accuracy of our estimates since the model operates on a snapshot of data from 2008.

## Summary

For researchers and policymakers in higher education, where the ages may typically range from 18-24 for college students and 25-34 for recent graduates, this method may be useful for estimating the undocumented population. However, it also comes with data limitations since conclusions drawn from downstream analyses based on this method may be misattributing correlations and effects of policy based on the characteristics of the undocumented population.

Though this conclusion is disappointing for social science and other fields of research (particularly in trying to inform policy), it may be reassuring to a population of people that may or may not want their immigration status to be identified in publicly available survey databases.
